title: Sparse response advisory protocol and SDK handoff notes
content:
Purpose
This doc collects a lightweight design for a Sparse Response Advisory Protocol (SRAP) and companion SDK ergonomics for low-bandwidth / edge-first clients. Goal: enable progressive structured output (JSON/typed frames) and tool-calls while keeping overhead minimal and making graceful fallbacks simple for mobile/IoT clients.

Why this is different
- Rather than full session snapshots or heavy streaming contracts, SRAP is an advisory header + tiny frame set that tells clients what to expect and how to resume/patch.
- Focus on minimal client CPU/network work: small control frames, optional fetch-on-demand for large tool results, and typed delta patches for structured fields.
- Optimizes for latency SLOs and for devices that may suspend/resume network (mobile).

Problem statement and motivating scenarios
- Mobile chat client must render intermediate summary and call a search tool; search results are large and occasionally delayed. Client should show a trustworthy placeholder and fetch the heavy payload only when needed.
- Low-bandwidth edge (satellite link) needs to avoid long-lived connections and wants concise hints about whether to open a stream or poll for results.
- Developers want deterministic SDK semantics for partial structured outputs (e.g., incremental JSON fields) without requiring them to implement complex patch reconciliation logic.

High-level goals
- Provide an advisory header that accompanies initial streaming chunks describing: fidelity_hint, tool_manifest, resume_cursor, estimated_additional_bytes.
- Define tiny frame types to represent: FIELD_PATCH, TOOL_SUMMARY, TOOL_HANDLE, FINAL_COMMIT, HEARTBEAT.
- SDK patterns: one-off callbacks for small frames, lazy fetch helpers for tool handles, patch-apply utilities with a strict patch ordering guarantee.
- SLO-friendly: default to low-latency shallow responses; allow explicit client opt-in to heavier fidelity.

Non-goals
- Do not attempt a full CRDT or OT layer — keep patch semantics linear and append-only for a session.
- Not a general-purpose streaming schema registry (we may point to Schema v2 later).

Protocol sketch (SRAP)
- Envelope: each response (streamed or not) begins with a micro-advisory JSON line (ASCII header) then zero or more frames. Header keys (compact names):
  - fh: fidelity_hint, values: low|mid|high (suggests expected completeness)
  - tm: tool_manifest (array of tool ids short form)
  - rc: resume_cursor (opaque token for resume/polling)
  - eb: estimated_bytes (decimal)
  - m: mode, values: streaming|pull|hybrid

- Frame canonical form (binary-safe): 
  [frame_type(1B)] [len(2B)] [payload(len)]
  frame_type enum: 0x01 FIELD_PATCH, 0x02 TOOL_SUMMARY, 0x03 TOOL_HANDLE, 0x04 FINAL_COMMIT, 0x05 HEARTBEAT

- FIELD_PATCH payload: path (dot) + op + value OR compact JSON Patch (RFC6902 subset). SDK will expose applyPatch(path, op, value) helpers.
- TOOL_SUMMARY payload: short text or compact JSON with tool id, latency_hint, checksum, small preview. Intended for immediate UX rendering.
- TOOL_HANDLE payload: opaque handle (URL or token) + small metadata. Clients can lazy-fetch full tool results via a secondary GET using the handle. Handles may be regional and short-lived.
- FINAL_COMMIT payload: final structured object digest + final resume_cursor=null

Example sequence (mobile chat)
1) Server sends advisory header: {"fh":"low","tm":["search.v2"],"rc":"c1-xyz","eb":"8k","m":"hybrid"}
2) Frames: FIELD_PATCH(title, set, "Quick summary of findings")
3) TOOL_SUMMARY(search.v2, latency_hint=120ms, preview=["hit1","hit2"])
4) FIELD_PATCH(results, append, [tool_handle: "h:abc123"])
5) HEARTBEAT frames intermittently
6) Later server sends TOOL_HANDLE payload: {"handle":"h:abc123","url":"https://rwd/api/tool-fetch/abc123?sig=...","size":5600}
7) FINAL_COMMIT digest

Client behavior (recommended SDK patterns)
- On header: choose mode. If fh==low and client is backgrounded, only render summary and schedule lazy fetch if user interacts.
- On TOOL_SUMMARY: show preview tiles (small).
- On TOOL_HANDLE: do a guarded fetch via sdk.fetchTool(handle, options) which supports: prefer-background-download, region, maxBytes threshold, cancellation token. SDK should automatically validate checksum if provided.
- On FIELD_PATCH: SDK exposes a deterministic api: session.applyPatch(seq_no, path, op, value). Patches must be idempotent when applied with sequence numbers and dropped-if-missing semantics are explicit.

Edge and offline considerations
- Resume: use resume_cursor with a soft TTL; session listing endpoint can return existing handles for a window.
- Polling fallback: for networks that don't support websockets, client can poll /session/{rc}/frames?since=seq_no. Server should return advisory header on first poll.
- Store-and-forward: small frames should be persisted by client to allow rehydration after suspend. Tool handles may be cached encrypted in local store for a short time.

SDK ergonomics (principles)
- Minimal surface area: callbacks for small frame types + small helper utilities (applyPatch, fetchTool, previewRenderer).
- Declarative wiring: developer registers renderers for typed fields, SDK wires patch application to the view layer via simple event bus.
- Backpressure and budget API: client can set budgets (bytes, time) and SDK will translate fh suggestions into actual fetch decisions.
- Safety-first: fetching tool handles should go through permission checks (app-level token) and be cancellable.

Telemetry and observability
- Telemetry keys to emit: advisory_mode_used, tool_handle_fetched, fetch_bytes, patch_apply_failures, resume_attempts, fallback_to_poll.
- Sampling: sample tool fetches for integrity checks and send ephemeral integrity pings (size/checksum/time).

Failures and graceful degradation
- Missing TOOL_HANDLE: SDK should show a small CTA to retry (developer-supplied).
- Patch conflict: if sequence gap detected, SDK should request /frames?since=last_seq to re-synchronize and mark the partial field as "stale" until resolved.
- Expired handles: server returns 410; SDK should surface concise reason and fall back to server-side summary (TOOL_SUMMARY).

Security and privacy notes
- Tool handles are short-lived signed URLs or opaque tokens scoped to session and client_id. Recommend rotating every 5–15 minutes for public URLs; shorter for very sensitive tools.
- Local caching must respect app-level PII policies. Provide a cache encrypted helper in SDK with configurable TTL.

Compatibility and migration notes
- Backwards compatibility: clients that don’t understand SRAP should ignore the advisory header and treat the stream as opaque text chunking. Therefore keep first-line header small and optional.
- Rollout: default to fh=low for 10% of traffic, collect telem for fetch rates and errors, then widen.

Open questions / trade-offs
- How much logic does the runtime perform server-side vs pushing to SDK? (eg. auto-expand handles when client is on wifi). Leave opt-in toggles for auto-fetch policies.
- Patch format: compact RFC6902 subset vs our tiny path/op/value tuple. RFC6902 is expressive but heavier to parse; we favor a small tuple for mobile but must keep server SDKs generating both.
- Tool handles as signed URL vs bearer token endpoint (proxy). Signed URL is simple for edge clients but requires RLS discipline. Proxy endpoints allow richer auth but more server cost.

Next steps and experiments
- Implement prototype SRAP encoder in serving runtime that can emit advisory header + frames for a subset of endpoints (chat + retrieval tool).
- Ship minimal client helpers in mobile-js SDK: applyPatch, fetchTool(handle, {budgetBytes, preferWifi}), and a demo showing lazy expansion on tap.
- Telemetry spike: measure percent of sessions that fetch handles, median fetch size, and extra latency introduced when fetching on demand vs in-line.
- Sizing: default estimate bytes heuristics and a server flag to force eager expansion for premium tenants.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally light-weight; I expect significant iteration. Focus review on: is the advisory header sufficient, do frame types cover common tool/case patterns, and are SDK helpers minimal enough?
- Links in linked_artifacts point to an early prototype PR and a Confluence sketch.

-- end of note --
